newsitem.title: CHINA: China cautions U.S. over Taiwan president trip.
newsitem.headline: China cautions U.S. over Taiwan president trip.

text.p: China called on Washington on Tuesday to ensure that Taiwan's president would not conduct activities harmful to unity of the motherland with his plans to transit through the United States.

"We hope the American side ... will not allow key Taiwan political figures to create 'two Chinas' or 'one China, one Taiwan' or conduct activities to split the motherland under the name of transitting the country," Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang said.
"Taiwan is the most important and sensitive question in Sino-U.S. relations," Tang told reporters at a regular news briefing.
Taipei said on Monday it would ask Washington to grant Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui a transit visa despite an expected protest from the island's arch rival, China.

Washington, which does not have official ties with Taiwan, said in April that Lee was eligible for a visa to transit through the United States on his way to a September conference in Panama, one of about 30 nations that recognises the island instead of communist Beijing.
Panama has invited Lee to attend a September 7-10 conference for users of the Panama Canal Zone, and Taipei views the meeting as a chance for Lee to rub shoulders with world leaders.

Beijing, which regards Taiwan as a rebel-ruled province and seeks to isolate its leaders from the international arena, was furious when Washington allowed Lee to visit his alma mater Cornell University in June 1995.
That visit sent Taiwan's slowly warming relations with the mainland into a tailspin and created new tensions in Sino-U.S. ties as well.

Beijing also held missile tests and war games near Taiwan in a bid to stifle a growing pro-independence mood on the island. That prompted Washington to send warships to seas around Taiwan in a show of force.
Beijing has also protested against U.S. decisions to grant transit or visiting visas to Taiwan's vice-president, foreign minister and other senior officials in the past.

Although China and Taiwan, split since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949, say they want eventual reunification, Beijing accuses Taipei of seeking international recognition and has threatened to invade if the island declares independence.
